newsitem.title: GERMANY: Accusations fly as Bonn gears up for budget debate.
newsitem.headline: Accusations fly as Bonn gears up for budget debate.

text.p: Accusations and resignation calls whizzed across Germany's political battleground as government and opposition geared up for a parliamentary showdown on Wednesday over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's budget policy.

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, the finance policy spokeswoman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said Waigel should quit in the wake of a humiliating climbdown last week, when the government had to postpone a planned tax cut.
"Someone who doesn't do their homework and makes promises he can't keep... is in the wrong job as finance minister," she told the Saechsische Zeitung newspaper.

But Bernd Protzner, the general secretary of Waigel's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), said SPD heads should roll for wasting taxpayers' money by forcing members of parliament back to Bonn for the "unnecessary" emergency debate.

One minister and several parliamentarians accompanying Chancellor Helmut Kohl on a tour of southeast Asia have cut short their trip to return to Bonn for the debate. Protzner said SPD parliamentary business manager Peter Struck was to blame.
"What the SPD is doing here is a blatant abuse of parliamentary rights," Protzner said in a statement. "That must have its consequences. I call on Struck to resign."

The sharp exchange followed a day after Bonn's finance policy took another body blow when six economic institutes predicted the 1997 budget deficit would miss the target laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for Europe's planned single currency.
Paul Kirchhof, a judge on the Federal Constitutional Court, also reminded Germans on Tuesday the supreme court had ruled in 1993 that the Maastrcht criteria must be strictly fulfilled.
The influential Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said the six institutes had ripped government finance policy apart.

"The coalition should take this as a sign that things can't go on as they did before," the conservative daily said in a front-page editorial. "Germany is in danger of staggering into a economic and social crisis."
The SPD has submitted a motion for the Wednesday afternoon debate, calling on parliament to state that Germany has moved out of "economic equilibrium".
Matthaeus-Maier said she wanted Waigel to come clean about how big the gaps in the current budget were.
"He certainly knows they're bigger than he's admitted up until now," she said. "If he doesn't, it's because he's paying more attention to leading the CSU than he is to the budget."

A row over how to plug holes in the budget brought the ruling coalition to the brink of collapse last week when the SPD used its majority in the upper house to block a government plan to delay a rise in child benefit payments.
To fill the gap, the government decided not to lower the widely unpopular "solidarity surcharge" on income tax by one percent in 1997 as it had promised.
The move enraged the liberal Free Democrat (FDP) junior coalition partners, who had long championed a cut in the tax, levied to help pay for the costs of German unification.
The FDP's economic policy spokesman, Otto Lambsdorff, even accused Waigel of presenting figures which at first glance looked as if they would not even add up.
